client: I've been having a really hard time since my mom passed away last year from cancer. I keep trying to push through at work, but I'll be sitting at my desk and suddenly I just can't concentrate on anything — my mind goes blank or I start thinking about her and lose track of everything. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try something because I can't keep going on like this.
therapist:
I'm really glad you reached out, and I want you to know that what you're carrying — grief, the pressure to keep functioning, and that sudden blankness that pulls you away — makes complete sense given the enormity of losing your mom. It takes real courage to try something new when you're not even sure it will help, and that willingness itself matters. 

Can you tell me a little more about what those moments at your desk feel like — is it more like your mind is pulling you *toward* memories of her, or more like it's shutting down to protect you from them?

client: Honestly, it's kind of both, but I think it leans more toward being pulled toward her — like I'll see a sticky note on my monitor and remember how she used to leave little notes around the house, and then I'm just... gone. It's not peaceful though, it's more like I get stuck in this loop of thinking about things I should have done differently, like whether I visited enough or said the right things near the end. And then the guilt kind of takes over and that's when my mind goes blank, like it can't handle processing all of it at once.
therapist:
What you're describing — being pulled in by a tender memory and then getting caught in that loop of "should haves" — is such a painful place to be, and that guilt you're feeling is actually a very common part of grief, even when someone loved as deeply and showed up as genuinely as you clearly did for your mom. Those "should have" thoughts are worth gently examining together, because grief has a way of making our minds focus on the gaps while overlooking all the ways we *were* there. 

When that loop starts and the guilt takes over, what does the voice in your head actually say to you — what's the specific thought that tends to hit hardest?

client: The thought that hits hardest is probably "you weren't there enough in the last few months" — like I kept telling myself I'd visit more once work slowed down, and it never did, and now there's no more time left to make that right. I replay specific moments where I chose work over driving up to see her, and it feels like evidence that I got my priorities wrong. I know on some level she understood, she never made me feel guilty about it, but that almost makes it worse somehow.
therapist:
That thought — "I wasn't there enough" — is carrying so much weight, and I want to gently notice something with you: you just said she never made you feel guilty, that she *understood*, and yet you're holding yourself to a standard even she wasn't holding you to, which tells me the harshest judge in this situation is you. It's also worth wondering whether "choosing work" was really a choice made carelessly, or whether you were doing what felt necessary at the time, without knowing time would run out when it did — our minds often rewrite those moments as selfish in hindsight, when they weren't. 

If your mom could hear the way you're speaking about yourself right now, what do you think she would want to say to you?

client: I know she'd probably tell me to stop being so hard on myself, that she was proud of me, something like that — she was always that way. But when I try to imagine her actually saying it, it feels a little hollow, like I'm just putting words in her mouth that I want to hear rather than something that would actually reach me. I guess I don't fully trust my own brain to give me comfort right now, if that makes sense.
therapist:
That makes complete sense, and it's actually a really honest and self-aware thing to notice — your mind is so exhausted from grief that it's even lost trust in itself, which can make comfort feel just out of reach no matter where it comes from. Rather than trying to manufacture comfort right now, I wonder if there's something more solid we could look at together — like whether there are people in your life, or even specific memories, that could serve as *outside* evidence of who you were to her, rather than relying on your worn-down mind to generate it on its own. 

Are there things she actually said to you, letters, messages, or even things others told you about how she spoke about you, that exist somewhere outside of your own head right now?

client: There are some text messages I haven't been able to bring myself to look at — she sent me a few in her last weeks that I read once and then kind of buried because they were too hard to sit with. My aunt also told me at the funeral that my mom talked about me all the time to her friends, said she was proud of everything I'd built. But I'm not sure going back to those messages is something I can actually do right now, it feels like it might just crack me open completely rather than help.
therapist:
Those messages and your aunt's words are real, external evidence that exists completely outside of your grieving mind's self-criticism — and the fact that you've kept those texts, even buried, feels significant, like a part of you is holding onto them until you're ready. The fear of being "cracked open" is worth respecting; we wouldn't want to rush toward them before you have some support around you, and there's actually something meaningful in just *knowing* they're there for when the time feels right. 

I'm curious — when you imagine a moment where you might feel ready to look at them, what would need to be different about how you're feeling, or what support would need to be in place, for that to feel safe enough?

client: I think I'd need to not be alone when I do it — that's the thing that scares me most, just sitting by myself in my apartment and falling apart with no one there. But the honest problem is that I don't really have someone like that right now, most of my close friends have kind of drifted since everything happened, and I haven't wanted to burden anyone with how bad it's actually been. So even identifying what I'd need doesn't feel like it gets me much closer, because I'm not sure that support is actually available to me.
therapist:
The loneliness you're describing — grieving your mom while also quietly grieving the drift of friendships, and carrying all of it alone so you don't burden anyone — that's a really heavy combination, and I want you to know that the isolation you're feeling isn't a reflection of how much people care about you, but more likely a result of grief making it hard to reach out and others not knowing how to show up. I also want to gently reflect something back: you said you haven't wanted to burden anyone with "how bad it's actually been," which tells me the people around you may not actually know the full weight of what you're carrying — and it's possible at least one of them would want to. 

If you think about even one person from before — a friend who's drifted, your aunt who spoke so warmly about your mom — is there someone who, if they truly knew how alone you've been feeling, you could imagine wanting to be there for you?

client: My aunt actually comes to mind — she checks in every few weeks with a text and I usually just say I'm doing okay, but she knew my mom better than almost anyone and she's never made me feel like I was too much. I guess I've been telling myself she has her own grief to deal with and doesn't need mine on top of it, but hearing you say it like that makes me wonder if I've been making that decision for her without actually asking. It still feels really vulnerable to think about being that honest with someone, like once I say out loud how bad it's been, I can't take it back.
therapist:
What you just noticed — that you've been protecting your aunt from a conversation she might actually want to have — is a really meaningful shift, and it takes courage to even consider that the story you've been telling yourself ("she has enough grief") might be something you assumed rather than something you know. That vulnerability you're describing, the feeling that saying it out loud makes it real and irreversible, is so understandable, but it's also worth considering that carrying this completely alone has its own cost that you've already been paying for a long time. 

What do you think a small, honest step might look like with her — not necessarily cracking everything open at once, but maybe something that lets her know you're not actually doing okay?

client: Maybe the next time she texts I could just say something like "actually, I've been struggling more than I've let on" instead of the usual "I'm fine" — that feels like it might be manageable without feeling like I'm dumping everything on her at once. But I'm already worried she'll ask follow-up questions and I won't know what to say, or I'll start crying and feel embarrassed about it. I think I've gotten so used to holding it together that even a small crack in that feels like it could spiral into something I can't control.
therapist:
That one sentence you described — "I've been struggling more than I've let on" — is actually a beautifully measured and honest step, and it gives your aunt an invitation without requiring you to have all the answers ready, because "I don't know how to put it into words yet" is a completely valid thing to say if she asks more. And I want to gently challenge the idea that crying or not having the right words means losing control — it might actually just mean that for once, you're letting someone see the truth of what you're carrying, which is different from spiraling. 

What would it mean for you if you did cry, or didn't have the perfect words — do you think your aunt would see that as too much, or is that more about how *you* would feel about yourself in that moment?

client: Honestly, I think it's more about how I'd feel about myself — my aunt would probably just hold space for it, she's that kind of person. But I have this deep discomfort with being seen as someone who can't cope, like I've built this whole identity around being the one who holds it together, and falling apart in front of someone feels like losing something I can't get back. I know that probably sounds irrational when I say it out loud, but it's a really strong feeling.
therapist:
It doesn't sound irrational at all — it sounds like "being the one who holds it together" has been a really important part of how you've understood yourself, maybe for a long time, and grief is asking you to loosen that in a way that feels like a loss of identity on top of everything else you're already losing. But I want to offer a gentle reframe: what if letting your aunt see you struggle isn't losing that strength, but actually a different expression of it — the kind that says "I know when I need someone, and I trust you enough to let you in"? 

I'm curious, when did "holding it together" become so central to who you are — is this something that started long before losing your mom, or do you think it's connected to her in some way?

client: It definitely started before losing her — I think I was the kid who didn't want to worry my parents, especially my mom, so I learned pretty early to handle things on my own and not make my problems someone else's burden. But now that you're asking, I'm realizing there's something almost painful about the fact that she was one of the few people I could occasionally let that guard down with, and now that's gone too. So maybe part of what I'm grieving isn't just her, but also the one safe place I had to not be okay.
therapist:
What you just named is profound and I want to make sure it lands — you're not only grieving your mom, you're grieving the one relationship where you didn't have to be the strong one, which means her death took something even deeper than her presence, it took your only sanctuary from yourself. That makes the weight of this so much clearer, and it also makes your isolation since losing her make complete sense, because the person you would have turned to *is* the loss itself. 

I wonder if, in a way, allowing your aunt in — someone who loved your mom and knows that version of you — might be the smallest possible step toward rebuilding a place where you don't have to hold everything together, not to replace what you had, but to honor that you still deserve to have somewhere safe to land?
